exercises.approach: Choose whole families first, A and B for training and C and D for assessment, and only then select their rows.
exercises.why: Each family holds two consecutive rows, so A and B cover ids 1 to 4 and C and D cover ids 5 to 8. No family can appear on both sides, which is the condition this fixture needs.
exercises.wrong: Drawing four row ids at random. With two rows per family, a random draw of four rows almost always takes one row from at least one family and leaves its sibling in assessment.

exercises.approach: Put odd rows in one partition and even rows in the other, then intersect the family labels as well as the ids.
exercises.why: Rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 carry A, B, C and D, and rows 2, 4, 6 and 8 carry the same four labels. The ids never overlap, yet every family is on both sides.
exercises.wrong: Checking only `intersect(d$id[row_train], d$id[row_test])`. It returns an empty vector and makes the split look clean while all four families leak.

exercises.approach: Loop over the four families, fit lm(y ~ x) on the other six rows, predict the two held out rows and store the fold count and squared error sum.
exercises.why: y = 1 + 2x holds exactly for all eight rows, so every fold recovers intercept 1 and slope 2 from its six rows, and each held out pair has zero error. The folds hold 2 rows each, 8 in total.
exercises.wrong: Fitting once on all eight rows and then splitting the errors by family. On this exact fixture the errors are still zero, so the leak is invisible in the output; only the per fold intersection check exposes it.

exercises.approach: Estimate the center from the training values 0 and 2 only, then subtract that same center from the held out values.
exercises.why: The training mean is 1, so 100 and 102 become 99 and 101. That transformation uses no held out information, so the assessment rows are treated as new data.
exercises.wrong: Centering all four values before splitting. The mean becomes 51 and the held out values become 49 and 51, so values the model should never have seen have shifted the center by 50.

exercises.approach: Cut the six days at day 4: days 1 to 4 train and days 5 and 6 assess.
exercises.why: The latest training day is 4 and the earliest assessment day is 5, so no later observation helps fit a predictor that is judged on later days.
exercises.wrong: Shuffling the six days before splitting. A shuffle can put day 6 in training and day 2 in assessment, so the model learns from the future it is meant to forecast.

exercises.approach: Add the error sums and the counts separately and divide once, then report the equal fold mean as a second, labeled figure.
exercises.why: The two folds hold 1 and 3 observations, so pooling gives (2 + 12) / 4 = 3.5. The per fold means are 2 and 4, and their plain average is 3.
exercises.wrong: Reporting the average of the fold means, 3, as the error per observation. It gives the single observation fold the same weight as the three observation fold and understates the pooled error by 0.5.

run_note: The starter holds eight rows with ids 1 to 8, four groups A to D of two rows each, and x values 0 to 7, and an empty results list. Run it and list which groups would appear on both sides of an alternating row split: all four would. Splitting by group instead keeps every group on one side, which is the partition a claim about new groups requires. Compute any centering constant from the training rows only.
checks_note: The assertions confirm that the grouped split shares no group between training and testing while the alternating split shares all four, that leave-one-group-out folds cover 8 rows with essentially zero error for the exact rule y equals 1 plus 2x, that a training-only center of 1 differs from a leaked mean of 51, that every training day precedes every test day, and that a pooled ratio of 3.5 differs from the mean of ratios, 3. They do not cover nested tuning.
